title: Energy changes in systems (specific heat capacity)

notes.definition: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius. The energy stored or released as temperature changes is ΔE = mcΔθ.
explanation: When a system is heated, the energy in its thermal store increases and its temperature usually rises. How much the temperature rises depends on three things: the mass of the substance, the type of material, and how much energy is supplied. The property of the material is called its specific heat capacity, c, measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C).

The change in thermal energy is given by ΔE = mcΔθ, where ΔE is in joules, m is in kilograms, c is in J/kg °C and Δθ is the temperature change in °C. This equation is given on the Physics equation sheet, so you need to be able to select it and use it, including rearranging to find c, m or Δθ. Δθ is always the change in temperature (final minus initial), not a single temperature reading.

Water has a very high specific heat capacity, 4200 J/kg °C. It takes 4200 J to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C, but only about 385 J to warm 1 kg of copper by 1 °C. So, for the same mass and energy, copper heats up about eleven times more than water. Materials with a high specific heat capacity store a lot of energy for a small temperature rise and release it slowly as they cool, which is why water is used in central heating systems and hot water bottles.

The same equation works for cooling. When a hot object cools, ΔE is the energy released from its thermal store to the surroundings. For example, 2 kg of water cooling by 50 °C releases 2 × 4200 × 50 = 420 000 J.

Required practical 1 determines the specific heat capacity of a material, usually a metal block or water. An electric heater transfers energy to a block of known mass; a joulemeter (or power × time) gives the energy transferred, and a thermometer gives the temperature rise. Rearranging gives c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ). Plotting temperature against energy transferred gives a straight line with gradient 1 ÷ (mc). Insulating the block reduces energy dissipated to the surroundings; without insulation the temperature rise is smaller, so the calculated value of c is too high.
keyFacts: Specific heat capacity: energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
ΔE = mcΔθ is given on the equation sheet.
Units: ΔE in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, Δθ in °C.
Water has a high specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C.
Substances with a low c (such as metals) heat up and cool down quickly for a given energy transfer.
Δθ is the temperature change (final temperature minus initial temperature).
Rearranged: c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ), m = ΔE ÷ (cΔθ), Δθ = ΔE ÷ (mc).
In the required practical, energy transferred is measured with a joulemeter or calculated from power × time.
Energy lost to the surroundings makes the measured c higher than the true value.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius, in J/kg °C.
The internal energy of a system; it increases when the system is heated.
The difference between the final and initial temperatures, in °C.
A meter that measures the energy transferred electrically to a device, in joules.
Material that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating, used to reduce energy lost to the surroundings.
How well energy can pass between two objects; a drop of water or oil in a thermometer hole improves it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think heat and temperature are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact temperature is a measure of how hot something is; the energy needed to change it depends on mass and specific heat capacity too.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use the final temperature as Δθ.
misconceptions.right: In fact Δθ is the change in temperature, final minus initial.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a material with a high specific heat capacity heats up quickly.
misconceptions.right: In fact a high c means more energy is needed per kg per °C, so it heats up slowly and cools down slowly.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think energy lost to the surroundings makes the calculated c too low.
misconceptions.right: In fact lost energy gives a smaller temperature rise for the energy measured, so c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ) comes out too high.

realWorld: Water is used in central heating radiators and hot water bottles because its high specific heat capacity lets it carry a lot of energy per kilogram.
Electric storage heaters contain dense blocks with a high specific heat capacity that are heated overnight and release energy slowly during the day.
Saucepans are made of metals with low specific heat capacity so they heat up quickly, while the sea warms and cools more slowly than land, keeping coastal climates milder.
examTips: Select ΔE = mcΔθ from the equation sheet and write it down before substituting.
Always work out Δθ as a difference first, and check whether mass is in g (divide by 1000).
If energy is given as power and time, calculate E = P × t with time in seconds.
For the required practical, explain that insulation reduces energy lost, and that losses make c too high.
The unit J/kg °C must be written in full for a unit mark.
summary: Specific heat capacity is the energy to raise 1 kg by 1 °C.
ΔE = mcΔθ (on the equation sheet); c in J/kg °C.
Water's c is high (4200 J/kg °C), so it stores lots of energy.
Rearrange to find c, m or Δθ; convert g to kg and kJ to J.
Required practical 1: heater, joulemeter, thermometer, insulated block.
Energy losses make the measured c larger than the true value.

questions.question: Which of the following is the definition of specific heat capacity?
options: The energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance
The temperature at which a substance boils
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
The energy stored in 1 kg of a substance
markScheme: 1 mark: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is per kilogram per degree Celsius. The energy to melt 1 kg is specific latent heat of fusion, a different quantity.

questions.question: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
options: J/kg °C
J/kg
J °C
W/kg
markScheme: 1 mark: J/kg °C
questions.explanation: c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ), so its unit is J ÷ (kg × °C) = J/kg °C. J/kg is the unit of specific latent heat.

questions.question:
The equation for the change in thermal energy of a substance is:
ΔE = m c Δθ
What does Δθ represent in this equation?
options: The final temperature
The specific heat capacity
The mass of the substance
The change in temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: The change in temperature
questions.explanation: The Δ symbol means 'change in'. Δθ is the final temperature minus the initial temperature.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about a sample of water and a block of copper.
The water and the copper are each supplied with 10 000 J of energy.
Which statement is correct?
options: The water has a larger temperature rise
The copper has a larger temperature rise
The water and the copper have the same temperature rise
Neither changes temperature because the masses are equal
markScheme: 1 mark: The copper has a larger temperature rise
questions.explanation: Δθ = ΔE ÷ (mc). Copper's much smaller c gives a much bigger Δθ: about 26 °C for copper compared with about 2.4 °C for water.

options: To make the block heat up more slowly so readings are easier
To stop the thermometer breaking
To reduce the energy dissipated to the surroundings
To increase the mass of the block
markScheme: 1 mark: To reduce the energy dissipated to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Insulation reduces energy transfer by heating from the block to the air, so more of the measured energy goes into raising the block's temperature and the value of c is more accurate.

questions.question:
A student determines the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
The student puts a few drops of water into the hole in the block that holds the thermometer.
What is the reason for this?
options: To improve thermal contact between the block and the thermometer
To cool the thermometer down
To increase the specific heat capacity of the block
To stop the block from rusting
markScheme: 1 mark: To improve thermal contact between the block and the thermometer
questions.explanation: Air is a poor conductor. Water fills the gaps so energy is transferred well to the thermometer, which then reads the block's true temperature.

questions.question:
A student determines the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block.
The student's value is higher than the accepted value.
What is the most likely reason for this?
options: The block was heated for too long
The thermometer was read too often
The joulemeter read zero at the start
Some energy was transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rise was smaller than expected
markScheme: 1 mark: Some energy was transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rise was smaller than expected
questions.explanation: c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ). The joulemeter counts all the energy supplied, but some is lost, so Δθ is smaller and c is calculated as too large. A zeroed joulemeter is correct practice.

questions.question: How does the energy needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 °C compare with the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 20 °C?
options: Twice as much is needed for the 2 kg sample
The same energy is needed for both
Half as much is needed for the 2 kg sample
Four times as much is needed for the 2 kg sample
markScheme: 1 mark: The same energy is needed for both
questions.explanation: ΔE = mcΔθ: 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J and 1 × 4200 × 20 = 84 000 J. The product mΔθ is 20 in both cases.

questions.question:
An electric storage heater has a core that is heated overnight. The core releases energy into the room during the day.
Which property of the core material is most important?
options: A low specific heat capacity, so it heats up quickly
A low density, so it is light
A high specific heat capacity, so it stores a lot of energy for each degree of temperature rise
A high thermal conductivity, so it releases all its energy quickly
markScheme: 1 mark: A high specific heat capacity, so it stores a lot of energy for each degree of temperature rise
questions.explanation: A high c means a large ΔE for a given mass and temperature rise, so the core stores a lot of energy and releases it as it cools. High conductivity would release it too quickly.

questions.question:
A student determines the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
Which piece of equipment does the student use to measure the temperature change of the block?
options: Ammeter
Joulemeter
Balance
Thermometer
markScheme: 1 mark: Thermometer
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature. The joulemeter measures energy transferred, the balance measures mass and an ammeter measures current.

questions.question:
Calculate the energy needed to increase the temperature of 1.0 kg of water by 10 °C.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C
markScheme: 1 mark: 42 000 J

questions.question:
A copper block of mass 0.50 kg is heated. The temperature of the block increases by 20 °C.
Calculate the energy transferred to the copper block.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Specific heat capacity of copper = 385 J/kg °C
markScheme: 1 mark: 3850 J

questions.question:
A mug contains 250 g of water at 15 °C. The water is heated to 95 °C.
Calculate the energy transferred to the water.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C
Give your answer in kilojoules.
markScheme: 1 mark: m = 0.25 kg and Δθ = 80 °C
1 mark: 84 kJ
questions.explanation: Convert 250 g to 0.25 kg and find Δθ = 95 − 15 = 80 °C. ΔE = 84 000 J, which is 84 kJ (divide by 1000).

questions.question:
A metal block of mass 2.0 kg is supplied with 36 kJ of energy. The temperature of the block increases by 20 °C.
Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
markScheme: 1 mark: ΔE = 36 000 J
1 mark: 900 J/kg °C
questions.explanation: Rearrange to c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ). 36 kJ = 36 000 J, so c = 36 000 ÷ 40 = 900 J/kg °C.

questions.question:
An iron pan of mass 0.80 kg is supplied with 7.2 kJ of energy.
Calculate the temperature increase of the pan.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Specific heat capacity of iron = 450 J/kg °C
markScheme: 1 mark: ΔE = 7200 J
1 mark: 20 °C
questions.explanation: Δθ = ΔE ÷ (mc) = 7200 ÷ 360 = 20 °C. Remember to convert kJ to J first.

questions.question:
1.5 kg of water at 18 °C is supplied with 315 kJ of energy. Assume no energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Calculate the final temperature of the water.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C
markScheme: 1 mark: Δθ = 50 °C
1 mark: final temperature = 18 + 50 = 68 °C
questions.explanation: The equation gives the temperature change, 50 °C. Add it to the starting temperature: 18 + 50 = 68 °C. Giving 50 °C is a common error.

questions.question:
A student used a 40 W heater to heat a 1.0 kg aluminium block for 10 minutes.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium from these results.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
markScheme: 1 mark: t = 600 s
1 mark: c = 24 000 ÷ (1.0 × 25) (temperature change = 45.0 − 20.0 = 25 °C)
1 mark: 960 J/kg °C
questions.explanation: 10 minutes = 600 s. Energy = power × time = 24 000 J. The temperature change from Table 1 is 45.0 − 20.0 = 25 °C. c = 24 000 ÷ (1.0 × 25) = 960 J/kg °C. This is above the accepted 900 J/kg °C because some energy was lost to the surroundings.

questions.question:
The water in a hot water bottle cools from 60 °C to 20 °C. The water releases 504 kJ of energy.
Calculate the mass of water in the hot water bottle.
Use the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C
markScheme: 1 mark: Δθ = 40 °C and ΔE = 504 000 J
1 mark: 3.0 kg
questions.explanation: m = ΔE ÷ (cΔθ) = 504 000 ÷ 168 000 = 3.0 kg. The equation works for cooling: ΔE is the energy released.

questions.question: What is meant by the specific heat capacity of a substance?
acceptedAnswers: energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C
energy needed to raise temperature of one kilogram by one degree Celsius
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
questions.explanation: Both 'one kilogram' and 'one degree Celsius' are needed for the mark.

questions.question:
A student determines the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
Name the meter that can be used to measure the energy transferred to the heater.
markScheme: 1 mark: joulemeter
questions.explanation: A joulemeter records energy transferred electrically in joules. Alternatively you can calculate energy from power × time.

questions.question:
A student determines the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
Name the instrument used to measure the mass of the block.
markScheme: 1 mark: (top pan) balance
questions.explanation: Mass is measured with a balance, in g or kg. Convert grams to kilograms before using ΔE = mcΔθ.

markScheme: 1 mark: the heater is hotter than the block (it still has energy in its thermal store)
1 mark: energy continues to be transferred by heating from the heater to the block until they reach the same temperature
questions.explanation: The heater element is hotter than the block. After the power is off it keeps transferring energy into the block, so you should record the highest temperature reached.

questions.question:
Hot water bottles are filled with water.
Explain why water is a good substance to use in a hot water bottle.
acceptedAnswers: releases a lot of energy as it cools
markScheme: 1 mark: water has a high specific heat capacity
1 mark: so it stores (and releases) a lot of energy for each degree it cools, keeping warm for a long time
questions.explanation: Each kilogram of water releases 4200 J for every 1 °C it cools, so a bottle of hot water gives out a large amount of energy slowly.

questions.question:
On a sunny day, the sand on a beach becomes much hotter than the sea. The sand and the sea receive the same energy per square metre from the Sun.
Suggest why the sand becomes hotter than the sea.
acceptedAnswers: sand has a lower specific heat capacity
water has a higher specific heat capacity
less energy needed to raise temperature of sand
markScheme: 1 mark: sand has a lower specific heat capacity than water
1 mark: so the same energy causes a larger temperature rise (Δθ = ΔE ÷ mc)
questions.explanation: With a lower c, less energy is needed per kg per °C, so sand warms more for the same energy input.

questions.question:
A student compares the specific heat capacities of different metal blocks.
Give two control variables in this investigation.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: mass of each block; power of the heater (or energy supplied); heating time; type and thickness of insulation; starting temperature
questions.explanation: To compare metals fairly, only the type of metal should change. The mass and the energy supplied affect the temperature rise, so they must be kept the same.

questions.question:
A student determined the specific heat capacity of aluminium.
Table 1 shows the student's value and the accepted value.
Explain why the student's value is too high.
Suggest one improvement to the method.
markScheme: 1 mark: some energy was dissipated to the surroundings (not all went into the block)
1 mark: so the temperature rise was smaller, and c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ) is too large

questions.explanation: The energy reading includes energy that escaped. Dividing by a smaller Δθ gives a larger c. Reducing losses brings the value closer to 900 J/kg °C.

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): gradient determined correctly, relationship between gradient and c explained and correct value calculated.

questions.explanation: From Figure 1 the temperature rises from 20 °C to 42 °C as 20 000 J is transferred, so the gradient is 22 ÷ 20 000 = 0.0011 °C/J. Rearranging ΔE = mcΔθ gives Δθ ÷ ΔE = 1 ÷ (mc). So c = 1 ÷ (1.0 × 0.0011) ≈ 910 J/kg °C, close to aluminium.

questions.question:
Electric storage heaters contain large blocks of material. The blocks are heated overnight. During the day the blocks release energy into the room.
Explain why the blocks are made of a material with a high specific heat capacity.
markScheme: Indicative content: specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C; a high c means a lot of energy is stored for each degree of temperature rise; using ΔE = mcΔθ, a large c gives a large ΔE for a given mass and temperature change; as the blocks cool they release this energy; so the heater can keep the room warm for many hours; the block does not need to reach a dangerously high temperature to store enough energy.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation linking high c to storing and releasing a large amount of energy, with reference to ΔE = mcΔθ or temperature change.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that a high c stores more energy, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: A high c lets a block store lots of energy for a modest temperature rise, and release it gradually as it cools, which suits heating a room through the day.
